report.tagline: The UK's largest home energy supplier, which wins customers with good service and smart tariffs, run on its own software platform called Kraken.
report.simpleSummary: Octopus Energy sells electricity and gas to homes, mostly in the UK. Everyone gets the same power through the same wires, so Octopus competes on price, service and smart tariffs that make electricity cheaper when you use it at the right time, like charging an electric car at night. It built its own software, Kraken, to run billing and customer service, and it now sells Kraken to other energy companies around the world. Kraken was split off as its own company in 2026.

overview.whatItDoes: Octopus buys electricity and gas on the wholesale market, or from its own wind and solar farms, and sells it to homes and businesses. It runs bills, smart meter data and support on Kraken. It sells heat pumps, solar panels and EV chargers too. It operates in the UK and several other countries, including Germany, Spain, Japan and the US.
howItWorks: A customer switches online in a few minutes; the old supplier is changed automatically.
A smart meter sends half-hourly readings, so Octopus can bill accurately and offer time-of-use tariffs.
Tariffs like Intelligent Octopus Go give cheap night rates for EV charging; Agile changes prices every half hour.
Saving Sessions pay customers to cut use at peak times, which saves Octopus buying expensive power.
Small teams of 'energy specialists' handle each customer group, with Kraken giving them the full account picture.
Kraken is licensed to other energy firms, who pay per customer account.
overview.valueProposition: For homes: fair prices, friendly human support and tariffs that reward using power when it is cheap and green. For energy firms: Kraken software that cuts the cost of serving each customer.

businessModel.summary: Octopus makes money from the small gap between what it pays for energy and what it charges customers, plus standing charges. Margins are thin, often around 1% to 3%. It earns more from software (Kraken licences), flexibility services to the grid, installs and its own generation.

revenueStreams.detail: Selling electricity and gas to homes and businesses; the vast majority of the roughly £13 billion revenue.
Per-account fees from energy firms using Kraken; now in a separate company.
Heat pumps, solar, batteries and EV chargers.
Its own renewable farms and payments for balancing the grid.

businessModel.pricing: Prices follow Ofgem's price cap for standard tariffs. Smart tariffs like Intelligent Octopus Go offer cheap night electricity; Agile rates change every half hour. Exact rates vary by region and are shown on octopus.energy.
costDrivers: Wholesale energy purchases, the biggest cost by far
Network and policy costs passed through
businessModel.unitEconomics: A typical UK home pays about £1,700 a year for energy under the price cap. Most of that goes on wholesale energy, network fees and government levies. Octopus might keep a margin of about 1% to 3%, so roughly £20 to £50 a year per home. The cost of serving that customer is the difference-maker: Kraken and fewer complaint calls let Octopus serve a home more cheaply than old rivals. That small saving per home across millions of homes is the business.

howTheyGetUsers: Taking on customers of failed suppliers, like Bulb
EV and heat pump owners seeking smart tariffs
whatBringsUsersBack: Energy is a monthly bill, so customers stay by default
Smart tariffs tied to their car, battery or heat pump
Good support makes switching away less appealing
growth.moat: Octopus's moat is Kraken: owning modern software lets it serve customers cheaper and launch new tariffs faster than rivals on old systems. Smart tariffs tied to home devices also make customers sticky. Price alone is not a moat, because energy is the same whoever sells it.

pmLessons: In a commodity market where the product is identical, service and pricing design become the product.
Building your own core software can turn a cost centre into a separate business, as Kraken shows.
Thin margins make cost to serve the key number; small savings per customer add up across millions.
Pricing can change behaviour: time-of-use tariffs shift demand in ways that help both users and the business.

interviewQuestions.question: Energy is the same from every supplier. How does Octopus win?
interviewQuestions.hint: Service, smart tariffs, cost to serve, referrals. Tie each to a metric.

interviewQuestions.question: Design a feature to get more customers to use power off-peak.
interviewQuestions.hint: Persona, behaviour barrier, incentive design (Saving Sessions), automation via devices. Metric: kWh shifted.

interviewQuestions.question: Should Octopus have spun off Kraken?
interviewQuestions.hint: Pros: neutral to rival utilities, capital raise. Cons: lose control. Consider licensee trust and valuation.

interviewQuestions.question: Customer complaints rose 20% this quarter. What do you do?
interviewQuestions.hint: Segment by type (billing, meters, payments), cohort (new vs old), and channel. Fix the biggest driver first.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the north star metric for Octopus?
interviewQuestions.hint: Homes saving money on smart tariffs. Break into supply, smart adoption, demand shifted, satisfaction.
